paper_title: Increased conjugated backbone twisting to improve carbonylated-functionalized polymer photovoltaic performance

knowledge_points.content: PBTCO-TT and PBTCO-T are conjugated polymers based on benzo[1,2-b:4,5-b′]dithiophene (BDT) and carbonylated thiophene units, differing only by the linker between the carbonylated units: thieno[3,2-b]thiophene (TT) for PBTCO-TT and thiophene (T) for PBTCO-T.
knowledge_points.evidence: In this work, we designed and synthesized two polymer donors, PBTCO-TT and PBTCO-T (Scheme 1), based on BDT and oligothiophene but with different linkers, T in the latter polymer and TT in the former, between two carbonylated thiophene units.

knowledge_points.content: The PBTCO-T:ITIC-based polymer solar cell achieved a power conversion efficiency (PCE) of 10.40%, with a Voc of 0.959 V, Jsc of 16.21 mA cm⁻², and FF of 66.89%.
knowledge_points.evidence: while the PBTCO-T:ITIC-based PSC showed a significantly higher PCE of 10.40% with simultaneous improvement of the VOC to 0.959 V, of the JSC to 16.21 mA cm−2 and of the FF to 66.89%.

knowledge_points.content: Replacing the thieno[3,2-b]thiophene (TT) unit with a thiophene (T) unit increases the twist angles of the polymer backbone, which suppresses excessive aggregation and improves the bulk heterojunction morphology in non-fullerene solar cells.
knowledge_points.evidence: Replacing the TT unit of PBTCO-TT with the T unit to form PBTCO-T resulted in weak aggregation in solution due to the greater torsions in the conjugated backbone. Such aggregation behaviour of PBTCO-T drove it to form a better BHJ morphology with ITIC than was formed by PBTCO-TT.

knowledge_points.content: PBTCO-TT and PBTCO-T exhibit nearly identical energy levels, with HOMO levels of -5.41 eV and -5.43 eV and LUMO levels of -3.56 eV and -3.55 eV, respectively.
knowledge_points.evidence: Cyclic voltammetry and density functional calculations confirmed similar molecular energy levels for the two polymers (HOMO/LUMO of −5.41/−3.56 eV for PBTCO-TT and −5.43/−3.55 eV for PBTCO-T).

knowledge_points.content: Temperature-dependent UV-Vis absorption indicates that PBTCO-TT has a stronger aggregation tendency than PBTCO-T, as PBTCO-TT maintains aggregation at 90 °C in chlorobenzene whereas PBTCO-T does not.
knowledge_points.evidence: at 90 °C, aggregation of PBTCO-TT still occurred but no aggregation was indicated for PBTCO-T, which implied a stronger tendency for PBTCO-TT than for PBTCO-T to aggregate in solution.

knowledge_points.content: DFT calculations at the B3LYP/6-31g (d, p) level reveal that PBTCO-T trimers have higher twist angles (up to 34.3°) compared to PBTCO-TT trimers (up to 25.6°).
knowledge_points.evidence: As shown in Fig. 3b, the three units of the trimer of PBTCO-TT showed twist angles of 12.8°, 25.0° and 25.6°, respectively. After replacing the TT units with T units, the resulting trimer of PBTCO-T exhibited a more twisted conjugated backbone with angles of 15.0°, 34.3° and 23.7°, respectively.

knowledge_points.content: PBTCO-T:ITIC blend films demonstrate a hole mobility (μh) of 1.15 × 10⁻⁴ cm² V⁻¹ s⁻¹ and an electron mobility (μe) of 3.78 × 10⁻⁴ cm² V⁻¹ s⁻¹, which are significantly higher than those of PBTCO-TT:ITIC.
knowledge_points.evidence: the μh of the PBTCO-T:ITIC film was 1.15 × 10−4 cm2 V−1 s−1, approximately two orders of magnitude higher than that of the PBTCO-TT:ITIC film (2.11 × 10−6 cm2 V−1 s−1). The μe of the PBTCO-T:ITIC film was 3.78 × 10−4 cm2 V−1 s−1, about two times higher than that of the PBTCO-TT:ITIC film (1.98 × 10−4 cm2 V−1 s−1).

knowledge_points.content: Charge transport in the PBTCO-T:ITIC device is more balanced with a μe/μh ratio of 3.3, whereas the PBTCO-TT:ITIC device is highly imbalanced with a ratio of 93.4.
knowledge_points.evidence: More importantly, the ratio of μe/μh was found to be more balanced for the PBTCO-T:ITIC film (3.3) than for the PBTCO-TT:ITIC film (93.4).

knowledge_points.content: The RMS surface roughness of the PBTCO-TT:ITIC blend film is 9.06 nm, which is much higher than the 1.51 nm measured for the PBTCO-T:ITIC film, indicating detrimental large-scale aggregation in the PBTCO-TT blend.
knowledge_points.evidence: After blending PBTCO-TT with ITIC, the RMS surface roughness value of the resulting PBTCO-TT:ITIC-based film sharply increased to 9.06 nm... In contrast, the PBTCO-T:ITIC film showed only a slightly higher RMS surface roughness (1.51 nm).

knowledge_points.content: The exciton dissociation probability (Pdiss) is 80.55% for the PBTCO-T:ITIC-based device and 60.62% for the PBTCO-TT:ITIC-based device, explaining the higher Jsc of the former.
knowledge_points.evidence: Pdiss was calculated to be 60.62% for the PBTCO-TT:ITIC-based device and 80.55% for the PBTCO-T:ITIC-based device. This result was in agreement with the J-V measurements showing a higher JSC value for the PBTCO-T:ITIC-based device.

knowledge_points.content: Both PBTCO-TT and PBTCO-T exhibit high thermal stability with 5% weight loss temperatures (Td) of 442 °C and 456 °C, respectively.
knowledge_points.evidence: The PBTCO-TT and PBTCO-T polymers both exhibited excellent thermal stabilities, with 5% weight loss temperatures (Td) of 442 and 456 °C, respectively.

knowledge_points.content: XRD analysis shows that PBTCO-T:ITIC blend films exhibit a strong π-π diffraction peak at 24.12° (0.37 nm), whereas PBTCO-TT:ITIC blend films show a strong chain-to-chain peak at 4.63° but a very weak π-π stacking peak.
knowledge_points.evidence: the PBTCO-TT:ITIC-based film showed a strong chain-to-chain diffraction peak at 4.63° (1.93 nm) and extremely weak π–π stacking peak. In contrast, the PBTCO-T:ITIC-based film showed a weak chain-to-chain diffraction peak at 4.51° (1.95 nm) and a strong π–π diffraction peak at 24.12° (ca. 0.37 nm).
